extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, news editors/producers, and researchers of audience behavior
extracted.subtask_short: news story selection for mass media
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for selecting and producing national news stories and magazine covers, emphasizing how audience characteristics, formal and informal feedback, commercial pressures, and professional norms shape editorial decisions. Covers both television news programs and weekly newsmagazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial considerations in cover/story selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors are aware that colleagues will be critical "if too many covers are chosen with commercial motives in mind"; they try to estimate newsstand sales figures for the next cover but "are as often wrong as they are right."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and anti-patterns: publishers know that certain topics sell (notably sex, health, and religion), and covers emphasizing 'pretty girls' generate sales but also staff and reader criticism. Editors may be reluctant to admit 'going commercial.' Sales estimates are used but are unreliable; tension exists between maximizing sales and maintaining editorial credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience demographics (age, sex, education, occupation, income)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience composition differs by medium: magazines tend to have more male, better-educated, higher-income readers with a median age in the mid-30s, whereas television news attracts slightly more women and a substantially older median audience (well over 50).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic data (e.g., Simmons/Nielsen tables) to inform targetting: tailor story topics, depth, and tone to the dominant demographic segments. Be aware of class- and occupation-related differences (professional/managerial vs. blue-collar/retired) when selecting stories and features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience regularity and attentiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The total audience contains both regular and irregular readers/viewers; only about a fifth of magazine readers look at every issue and a twentieth of viewers see every program, though over 60% see at least half. Self-reported attention is higher than observed undivided attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan content assuming many audience members skim or attend partially. Recognize that reading/viewing frequency varies by education, age, and sex (e.g., magazine regularity higher among college graduates; TV regularity higher among older, less-educated viewers). Design stories/segments to engage intermittent and distracted users (clear leads, salient visuals, personally relevant hooks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal audience research and ratings, but treat findings critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have access to ratings, circulation figures, and audience studies but often reject or mistrust them. Research can report recurring patterns but may not resolve decisions about individual stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research to identify broad patterns (topics that attract attention, anchorperson appeal), but be cautious about overgeneralizing small-sample pilot studies. Anticipate professional skepticism and the risk that research findings may be interpreted or used by nonjournalistic managers to push commercial formats. Research is most useful when it complements, not supplants, editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond promptly and seriously to letters reporting factual mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters that describe factual mistakes are read carefully; unexpected surges in critical mail (or mail on atypical topics) are also taken seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain processes to verify and correct factual errors flagged by audience mail. Distinguish between routine critical mail (often dismissed) and credible complaints about accuracy; the latter should trigger review and correction to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and avoid violating cultural taste taboos (profanity, sacrilege, sex)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The principal targets of indignation are profanity, sacrilege, politics, and above all, sex." Sensitive subjects—especially sexualized covers—have produced large letter-writing backlashes and subscription cancellations (e.g., Time's Last Tango in Paris cover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often preempt backlash by observing taste taboos. Consider likely audience reactions to provocative imagery or language; use cover placement and prominence judiciously. Be aware that tolerance can change over time (some formerly controversial imagery later drew fewer complaints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that letter writers are atypical of the total audience
rubrics_metrics.description: People who write letters tend to be older, better-educated, more affluent, politically more conservative, and more civically involved than nonwriters; television mail also includes a higher proportion of mentally disturbed or 'crank' correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate volume or tone of mail with majority opinion. Assess representativeness before altering coverage. Use sampling or research to determine whether correspondence reflects broader audience sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance professional news judgment against audience wants — preserve editorial autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists assert that "you can't edit by readership survey, so we have to take the lead," believing their professional judgment should determine what the audience needs rather than simply what it wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a professional standard that can override short-term audience preferences when necessary for public-interest reporting. However, be open to credible evidence of audience need or harm; preserve autonomy but avoid paternalism that ignores demonstrable audience relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use informal/internal feedback (superiors, colleagues) as primary editorial input
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often 'film and write for their superiors and for themselves,' relying on internal product considerations and the known 'cell' audience (office staff, family) rather than the unknown mass audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop internal review and editorial-feedback mechanisms (editors, producers, peers) as primary checks on story selection and presentation. Recognize the limits of this inward-looking feedback and complement it with periodic external measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate audience uses of national news (reassurance, practical relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people use national news to be reassured the world is safe or to learn about topics that affect their lives (economy, health); most are more interested in local, personally relevant news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame national stories to highlight practical implications for different micro-societies where possible (e.g., how a national policy might affect localities, income groups). Provide context and human-scale relevance to increase perceived usefulness and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect ideological skew in correspondence and adjust interpretation accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Mail is often dominated by cultural and political conservatives; liberals write less often. During major events (e.g., Watergate), mail volumes and partisan direction can surge dramatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating criticism, account for ideological bias in letter writers and for episodic spikes tied to salient events. Use balanced measurement (polls, representative audience studies) before making editorial changes based solely on ideological mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of researchers' institutional motives and managerial misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are suspicious that audience research may be under business control and could be used by nonjournalists to push sensationalism or to evaluate journalistic autonomy; researchers themselves may be career-pressured to please management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on methodological transparency and independence of research. Use findings presented as objective evidence and guard against managerial mandates that would compromise editorial standards. Researchers may increase acceptance by avoiding prescriptive recommendations that undermine journalists' authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply audience research selectively where it can improve competitive performance (formats, anchor appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience research has sometimes driven personnel and format changes (e.g., hiring an anchorperson shown to have audience appeal; local format changes after studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage research for decision areas where measurable audience response matters (anchor selection, presentation format, pacing). Treat research as one input among editorial, ethical, and business considerations; use larger, well-funded studies where management decisions hinge on findings.
